Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra
stories.text:
Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi.

Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073. It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races.

Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself.

At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans.

There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack.

Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc).

When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI.

We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead.

You can get started with `npm create factory`.

It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think!

https://factory.mastra.ai

https://github.com/mastra-ai/template-factory

Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
stories.text:
Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook (https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com).

Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community.

Here’s a demo video: (https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM)

If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild.

We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do.

More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state).

Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862, August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449, May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code.

How it works…

Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal.

When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas.

The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant.

Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is.

This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection – which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt.

We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They’re almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I’ve made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that’s already been built.

The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook.com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams.

We'd love to hear which repos work and which don't, what you try to do on the canvas, and what's missing. We’re so excited for this to be a new way for designers to work in code!

The Onlook team (Joel - thebrubaker and Kris - krisodd), and I will be here all day!

Show HN: Foolscap – a writing app that reads your book and never writes for you
stories.text:
People are scared of their ability to write and think atrophying, so I wondered: what if I built something that enhanced human creativity instead of destroying it by doing the thinking and writing for people? Foolscap is the result, or at least the first version of that idea that's fleshed out enough to share here.

It reads as you write and picks out the structure: characters, ideas, threads, what's left hanging. You can respond to what it picks out, so there's a dialectic between the system and you as the writer. There's also an agent on the side, plugged into the same system, so you can ask about your book and fire off actions through conversation. It never writes into your work.

The system can also follow theorems and proofs and string together their dependencies, but I haven't made that a focus yet. There's no Lean support, for example. If anyone's interested in that, I'd love to hear it.

I want to build this by iterating with the people who use it: a tool that uses AI not to bypass the creative process, but to bring new tools to it. There's a free tier, and if you email hello@foolscap.works I'll send you a code for 50% off. This is my first product, so feedback of any kind is welcome.

Thanks, David

Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents
stories.text:
Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime (https://maritime.sh). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents.

Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY

There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is:

You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins.

It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem.

We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction:

1. Agent lifecycle management.

There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime. There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up.

2. Custom environments.

Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies. Some agents need access to private networks to interact with customer-specific things on prem, or residential IPs, or the ability to restrict network access completely.

3. Cost optimization.

If you’re selling a personal assistant for $20/month, a sandbox that costs $0.04/hour comes out to roughly $29/month if you keep it running continuously, not including LLM inference, storage, etc. There is a way to combat this though, which is to optimize sandbox usage with auto-snapshotting, making things event-driven, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, cold-tiering snapshots, etc. All roads lead to… building more infrastructure.

So what did we build differently?

We give each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. On top of the compute, we built a lot of composable services: provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking, login handoffs, all the things you’d need for production agents.

We also spent a huge amount of time optimizing cost. A lot of thought was put into things such as scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering, and other optimizations while balancing these with performance metrics like latency.

As a result, Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month (unlimited usage for that $1), with additional resources available as needed.

Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure. Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. We started Maritime together this March because of all the issues we faced with trying to deploy agents to the cloud during our research.

We want your feedback.

If you're building an agent product, what did you have to build on top of sandboxes to make them work? We want to know about all the workarounds and weird things you’ve had to build.

Are there things you’ve tried to build with VMs but couldn’t? Does Maritime fit your needs? Is there a feature we’re missing that would make us more enticing?

Happy to answer any questions in the comments.

https://maritime.sh

Show HN: Robotics needs better CAD, so I wrote a B-rep kernel and 3,487 tests
stories.text:
Hey HN, I’m Tony. I’m a co-founder of Springcraft, where we have been doing a lot of CAD modeling for robot parts. Our team kept running into limitations with existing kernels, and so I decided to write a new B-rep kernel and a new comprehensive, kernel-agnostic B-rep conformance test suite. Both are available today under MIT licenses.

The kernel, springrep, is written in safe Rust with no dependencies. It covers a broad range of our mechanical CAD needs, including advanced fillets, sweeps, lofts, shells, offsets, STEP and exact measurements and queries. Claude Code made it feasible to write this, but it took a lot of time and care to get it right.

The test suite, brep-conformance, has 3,487 cases covering the modeling operations common across kernels: booleans, fillets, chamfers, shells, offsets, sweeps, lofts, STEP, and queries with expected answers coming from closed forms and exact geometry. It caught hundreds of bugs, edge cases, and hot spots in springrep that our own tests had missed, and now springrep passes all of it. We’ve also run it on a few popular open-source kernels and anyone can run it on theirs. This is the first version, so there are surely mistakes in the test and adapters. Corrections, pull requests, and new kernels are welcome.

kernel: https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep conformance suite: https://springcraft-ai.github.io/brep-conformance/

Claude Gets Hella Paranoid
stories.text:
Mm, so I hesitate to write this, because my own AI agents might read it. But what the hell.

I've got this crappy little $300 PC on my network hooked up to my projector, that I mostly use to serve Jellyfin. So tired of it going down every time there's a Windows update, but I've been too lazy to get around to installing Ubuntu. Last night, when it went down, I asked my Claude-claw via Whatsapp if it could just SSH into it and set up a dual boot partition.

Claude got as far as partitioning the drive and then starting asking hard questions, like (paraphrasing) "wait a minute. This crosses a line. I have now been asked to remote into a machine with a password, write a separate boot partition, and restart it. From this chat, you haven't really verified that you are you. If you're really there, and not just texting me, give me some proof".

So I remoted in and created a TextEdit RTF file on the claw's desktop: "Hey, it's me, I'm asking you to remote into the PC".

Claude read it and responded that it was the kind of proof it was looking for, real RTF headers and datestamps and such. I had proven I had physical access to the claw machine, (although not to the PC, but it seemed reassured anyway). A little while later, before triggering the Ubuntu installer, it put me through it all over again. I told Claude I was very thankful it was guarding my network so well, and I would go over and write a file on the target PC manually too.

I'm not gonna lie: It was very fucking cool that it was able to do this without me ever needing to flash a USB drive, and by the time it was done it had set up Ubuntu, Tailscale and Jellyfin, and resolved the network issues; when I started watching a movie, the sound didn't work, so I prompted it and suddenly the sound came on as it wired up the HDMI adapter. Almost creepy.

But I was pretty stunned at how reticent it was to do something relatively simple on my own network, with access I gave it. I think there must be a serious push right now to lock it down from monkeying with anything remotely, especially a BIOS.

Ask HN: Where do you see Software in 5 years?
stories.text:
I wanted to hear some good opinions on all things AI and how they transform the Software industry. I'm anxious about the future and lack the foresight to form any opinion on what to do next.

For context, I'm a L4 SWE that has more or less say 5-10 yrs of exp.

I've enjoyed my work throughout my career, AI makes me ship more, much more than I could do 3 years ago. I feel I use it well and it translates into really good software.

That said, what do you think happens in years to come with the Software industry in general? Do you think we'll go through a massive erosion of jobs? What's your perspective on that?

I'm asking because I honestly don't know what to do: I can try to always keep up to date with newest technologies, best practices, but I'm only me; if the demand for SWEs and jobs falls to the floor, I'm not sure I'll always get a place at the table (i.e. land a job) and I'm wondering whether I should try to do something else in some other industry. It feels weird to be in a good position in life and still constantly worry about it getting worse.

Show HN: Zpup – Zdog style 3D scenes in JSON, SVG from any angle
stories.text:
Hi. I made small project called Zpup. It takes small 3D scene written in JSON and gives back a flat SVG from any angle. There is no JavaScript in the file, so it works in img-tag or README.

I needed 3D for small project at my company, and Zdog make big impression on me. But Zdog has not had a release for several years, so I wanted to make modern version.

One thing works different. Zdog sorts each shape by one point. so small thing on big floor gets covered when you turn it. Zpup compares the shapes that overlap. You can see both in the README.

I wrote it with Claude Code Fable 5.2.

No canvas renderer, no text shape, and it is 0.2 version.

Playground: https://rxolve.github.io/zpup

Feedback is always welcome :)
